runtime_proof.harness: Two production builds of the Command Center, served by `next start` and probed over real HTTP with curl. The two arms differ in exactly one line of one file -- the middleware matcher -- and in nothing else; see runtime_proof.build_identities for the sha256 of each built source and the one-line diff between them. Probing a served build is the only way to observe this defect: Next's `config.matcher` decides whether middleware is invoked at all, so a test that calls `middleware()` directly cannot see it, and every such test passed while the bypass was live.

queries.name: an anonymous dotted-path request to a dynamic route is refused
queries.method: GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/picks/abc.def with no credentials, against each arm
queries.result: arm B (original matcher): HTTP 200, Content-Type text/html, body begins '<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en" class="dark">' -- the operator page rendered. arm A (fixed): HTTP 401, Content-Type application/json, body {"ok":false,"error":{"code":"COMMAND_CENTER_AUTH_REQUIRED",...}}, with a WWW-Authenticate challenge and x-request-id set by the middleware.
queries.significance: This is the exposure, observed rather than inferred. Under the original matcher Next never invoked middleware for this path, so authentication was skipped entirely -- not evaluated and allowed. The page's server components hold service-role database access.

queries.name: the same route without a dot was already refused, in both arms
queries.method: GET http://127.0.0.1:<port>/picks/abc with no credentials, against each arm
queries.result: 401 in both arms, identical JSON refusal body.
queries.significance: Establishes that the defect was the URL's shape and nothing else. The route, the handler and the auth decision function were all unchanged; only whether middleware ran at all differed.

queries.name: an anonymous Next-Action POST to the dotted path -- stated limitation
queries.method: POST http://127.0.0.1:<port>/picks/abc.def carrying a Next-Action header with a FABRICATED 40-hex action id and an empty JSON array body, against each arm
queries.result: arm B (original matcher): HTTP 404, header 'x-nextjs-action-not-found: 1', body 'Server action not found.' -- Next rejected the fabricated id before dispatch. arm A (fixed): HTTP 401 with the same JSON refusal as the GET.
queries.significance: This demonstrates rejection at the authentication boundary: with the fix the request never reaches the action dispatcher. It does NOT prove anonymous execution of a real server action, because the action id was fabricated and Next declined it on that ground alone in the control arm. The remaining server-action coverage is attributed to the source tests and mutations recorded under static_proof.mutation_control, not to this probe.
queries.limitation: stated, not resolved -- see static_proof.mutation_control entries M2 through M8 for what does constrain the server-action surface

queries.name: the correctly-configured path is preserved
queries.method: GET / , /picks/abc and /picks/abc.def with 'Authorization: Bearer <redacted-probe-token>' against arm A
queries.result: 200 in all three cases; /picks/abc.def returns the rendered operator page with Content-Type text/html.
queries.significance: The fix refuses anonymous callers without refusing authenticated ones. Requirement 5 of the issue, measured rather than asserted.

queries.name: public paths stay public under the narrowed matcher
queries.method: GET /api/health and /icon.svg with no credentials, against each arm
queries.significance: Narrowing the matcher to Next's build output moved the public/private decision into isPublicPath without changing which paths are actually public.
